title: Arbores motae. Cyparissus
titleEn: The trees that came, and Cyparissus — Metamorphoses X.86–142
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 8719b7d375018d4f. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: A grassy, level hilltop has no shade until a singer born of gods sits down on it and sets his strings sounding; then the trees come, one after another, most of them given a single epithet and nothing more, though the pine is called dear to the mother of the gods because Attis hardened into it. Among them is the cypress, which was once a boy: Cyparissus, loved by the god who tunes both lyre and bow, and devoted to a great tame stag of the Carthaean fields, its horns gilded, its neck hung with jewelled collars, unafraid of any hand. He kills it with a javelin without meaning to, is not consoled, and asks the gods for one last gift — to mourn for ever.

sentences.t:
Collis erat collemque super planissima campi
area, quam viridem faciebant graminis herbae.
sentences.l: There was a hill, and above the hill a wholly level stretch of open field, which the blades of grass were making green.
sentences.i: There was a hill, and on top of it a perfectly level open space, which the growing grass kept green.
sentences.n: super follows its accusative in collemque super, a postposed preposition that verse allows. area campi is the level ground of the hilltop, and the superlative planissima makes it as flat as ground gets. quam is the relative picking up area, and faciebant is imperfect: the grass was keeping it green as a standing state, not doing so at one moment.

sentences.t: Umbra loco deerat:
sentences.l: Shade was lacking to the place:
sentences.i: The place had no shade:
sentences.n: deerat, from desum, governs the dative loco: Latin says the shade was lacking to the place where English says the place had none. The colon holds the sentence open for the answer that will close it.

sentences.t:
qua postquam parte resedit
dis genitus vates et fila sonantia movit,
umbra loco venit.
sentences.l: in which part, after the bard begotten of gods had sat down and had moved the sounding strings, shade came to the place.
sentences.i: and once the god-born singer had settled there and set the strings sounding, shade came to the place.
sentences.n: postquam stands inside the relative phrase qua ... parte, “in which part”, so the Latin runs literally “in which part after he sat down”. dis genitus is “born of gods”, an ablative of origin with the participle of gigno; the lines do not name the singer, and nothing here says which gods. Both resedit and movit hang on the one postquam. The clause answers the colon by giving back the same two words with the verb reversed: umbra loco deerat, umbra loco venit.

sentences.t: Non Chaonis afuit arbor.
sentences.l: The Chaonian tree was not absent.
sentences.i: The Chaonian tree did not stay away.
sentences.n: afuit, “was away”, opens a run of negatives that carries the whole catalogue: every tree is named as one that was not missing. Chaonis is simply “Chaonian”, from Chaonia in Epirus, and the epithet is the only identification the line offers; no story is told about the tree here. The edition prints a full stop after arbor and then goes on with lower-case non — and four words earlier, after venit., it printed a capital Non. The negatives that follow have no finite verb of their own and take over this afuit by ellipsis; that would be true whatever the punctuation, and the text is given here exactly as the edition prints it.

sentences.t:
non nemus Heliadum, non frondibus aesculus altis,
nec tiliae molles, nec fagus et innuba laurus,
sentences.l: not the grove of the Heliades, not the aesculus with its high foliage, nor the soft lindens, nor the beech and the unwed laurel,
sentences.i: nor the grove of the Heliades, nor the aesculus with its foliage high above, nor the soft lime trees, nor the beech, nor the unwed laurel,
sentences.n: The negatives keep running, non ... non ... nec ... nec, all still governed by the afuit before them. nemus Heliadum is “the grove of the Heliades”, the Sun's daughters; they are named and nothing further is said of them. frondibus altis is an ablative of description with aesculus, a kind of oak identified here only by its high leafage. innuba is “unwed”, from in- and nubo, “to veil oneself as a bride”, and it is the whole of what the line says about the laurel.

sentences.t:
et coryli fragiles et fraxinus utilis hastis
enodisque abies curvataque glandibus ilex
et platanus genialis acerque coloribus impar
amnicolaeque simul salices et aquatica lotos
perpetuoque virens buxum tenuesque myricae
et bicolor myrtus et bacis caerula tinus.
sentences.l: and the brittle hazels and the ash useful for spears and the knotless fir and the holm-oak bent down by its acorns and the festive plane and the maple unequal in its colours and, along with them, the river-dwelling willows and the watery lotus and the box green without end and the slender tamarisks and the two-coloured myrtle and the tinus dark-blue with berries.
sentences.i: and brittle hazels, and the ash that is good for spears, and the fir without a knot in it, and the holm-oak bent under its acorns, and the plane that belongs to feast days, and the maple with its uneven colouring, and with them the willows that live beside rivers, and the lotus that grows in water, and box that stays green all the year, and slender tamarisks, and the myrtle of two colours, and the tinus dark blue with its berries.
sentences.n: One connective after another, et and -que, carries a dozen trees, and the string still hangs on that same afuit. Each gets one epithet and no more: hastis is a dative with utilis, “useful for spears”; enodis is “without knots”; curvata glandibus is “bent by its acorns”, an ablative of cause; genialis belongs to the Genius and so to feasting and pleasure; coloribus impar is “unequal as to its colours”, an ablative of respect; amnicola is a compound, “river-dwelling”; bicolor is “of two colours”. tinus is left in Latin here, as aesculus was above: the line pins it only by its dark berries, and naming one modern species would claim more than the text does. The edition prints no stop anywhere between hastis and tinus, which is why this runs as one long unit.

sentences.t:
Vos quoque, flexipedes hederae, venistis et una
pampineae vites et amictae vitibus ulmi,
sentences.l: You too came, you bending-footed ivies, and along with you the vine-leafed vines and the elms clothed in vines,
sentences.i: You came too, ivies with your winding feet, and with you the leafy vines and the elms wrapped in them,
sentences.n: The list breaks off into apostrophe: the poet stops naming trees and speaks to them, vos ... venistis in the second person. quoque here is the plain adverb “also”, not the ablative of the relative. flexipedes is a compound of flexus and pes, “bending-footed”, describing the way ivy travels. una is the adverb “together”, not the numeral. amictae vitibus is “clothed with vines”, the elm wearing the vine that climbs it.

sentences.t:
ornique et piceae pomoque onerata rubenti
arbutus et lentae, victoris praemia, palmae
et succincta comas hirsutaque vertice pinus,
grata deum matri;
sentences.l: and the manna-ashes and the pitch-pines and the arbutus loaded with its reddening fruit and the pliant palms, the victor's prizes, and the pine, girt as to her foliage and shaggy at the crown, dear to the mother of the gods;
sentences.i: and manna-ashes and pitch-pines, and the arbutus weighed down with reddening fruit, and the supple palms that are a winner's prize, and the pine with its foliage drawn in and its crown shaggy, dear to the mother of the gods;
sentences.n: comas after succincta is a Greek accusative of respect: the pine is “girt as to her foliage”, the accusative naming the part concerned, and vertice does the same work in the ablative, “shaggy at the crown”. victoris praemia stands in apposition to palmae — the palm is what a winner is handed. deum is the older genitive plural for deorum, so deum matri is “to the mother of the gods”.

sentences.t:
siquidem Cybeleius Attis
exuit hac hominem truncoque induruit illo.
sentences.l: seeing that Cybelean Attis put off the man in this tree, and grew hard in that trunk.
sentences.i: for it was in this tree that Cybele's Attis put off his human shape, and into that trunk that he stiffened.
sentences.n: siquidem, “seeing that”, gives the reason for grata deum matri: the pine is dear to Cybele because Attis became one. exuit hominem is “put off the man”, the human shape handled as a garment to be taken off. hac and illo are ablatives pointing at the pine and at its trunk, and induruit is intransitive, “grew hard”. Cybeleius is “of Cybele”; the line says that Attis was hers and that he hardened into the tree, and tells none of the rest of his story.

sentences.t: Adfuit huic turbae metas imitata cupressus,
sentences.l: There was present at this throng the cypress that had copied the turning-posts,
sentences.i: Into this crowd came the cypress, which takes the shape of a race-track turning-post,
sentences.n: adfuit takes the dative huic turbae, “was present to this throng”. imitata is the perfect participle of imitor, a deponent — passive in form, active in meaning — so it is the cypress that does the imitating, not the cypress that is imitated. metae are the cone-shaped posts at each end of a Roman race-track, and the likeness is one of shape: a tapering point.

sentences.t:
nunc arbor, puer ante deo dilectus ab illo,
qui citharam nervis et nervis temperat arcum.
sentences.l: now a tree, before a boy loved by that god who with strings tunes the lyre and with strings the bow.
sentences.i: now a tree, before that a boy, loved by the god who tunes the lyre by its strings and the bow by its string.
sentences.n: nunc ... ante sets the present tree against the earlier boy before the sentence says anything else about either. dilectus ab illo deo is “loved by that god”: the Latin states the love and identifies the god not by a name but by his two instruments. nervis stands in the same case in both halves, citharam nervis et nervis ... arcum, so that one word serves for lyre-string and bowstring, and the two accusatives sit at the outer edges with the two ablatives at the centre. temperat is “brings to the right pitch”, used here of the bow as well.

sentences.t:
Namque sacer nymphis Carthaea tenentibus arva
ingens cervus erat,
sentences.l: For, sacred to the nymphs that hold the Carthaean fields, there was a huge stag,
sentences.i: For there was a great stag, sacred to the nymphs who hold the fields of Carthaea,
sentences.n: Namque, “for indeed”, opens the explanation of how a tree came to have been a boy. sacer governs the dative nymphis ... tenentibus, “sacred to the nymphs holding”. Carthaea arva names the territory of Carthaea, and the adjective is all the geography the sentence gives. The clause keeps its verb to the end, ingens cervus erat, so the size lands before the animal does.

sentences.t:
lateque patentibus altas
ipse suo capiti praebebat cornibus umbras.
sentences.l: and with widely spreading horns he himself was furnishing deep shade for his own head.
sentences.i: his antlers spread wide, and he made deep shade for his own head with them.
sentences.n: The two phrases are interlocked, ablative and accusative alternating — lateque patentibus, altas, then cornibus, umbras — with the verb and its dative sitting between them. capiti is the dative of the one served, “for his own head”, and ipse insists that he needed nothing but himself for shade. The imperfect praebebat makes it a standing habit. The noun is the same umbra that the hilltop had lacked and then received.

sentences.t:
Cornua fulgebant auro, demissaque in armos
pendebant tereti gemmata monilia collo.
sentences.l: His horns were shining with gold, and jewelled collars, let down onto his shoulders, were hanging on his rounded neck.
sentences.i: His antlers gleamed with gold, and jewelled collars dropped over his shoulders and hung from his smooth neck.
sentences.n: auro is an ablative of means with fulgebant: the horns are gilded, not gold. gemmata is “set with gems”. demissa in armos comes before the verb and tereti ... collo after it, that second phrase splitting open to enclose its own subject, gemmata monilia. teres is “smoothly rounded”, said of anything turned true.

sentences.t:
Bulla super frontem parvis argentea loris
vincta movebatur parilique aetate:
sentences.l: A silver boss above his forehead, bound on with small straps, kept swaying, and it was of an age with him:
sentences.i: A silver stud above his brow, fastened with little thongs, swung as he moved, and it was as old as he was:
sentences.n: bulla is the boss a Roman boy wore round his neck until he came of age, and the stag has been given one. vincta, “bound”, agrees with bulla and takes the ablative parvis ... loris, “with small straps”. parili aetate is an ablative of description: the ornament is of an age with the animal, so it has been on him since he was small. Magnus prints parilique aetate; some editions print parilesque ex aere, which instead makes the following clause say that matching ornaments of bronze shone, and takes the age out of the sentence altogether.

sentences.t:
nitebant
auribus e geminis circum cava tempora bacae.
sentences.l: pearls were shining from his twin ears around his hollow temples.
sentences.i: from his two ears pearls gleamed about his hollow temples.
sentences.n: bacae are berries, and by transfer the pearls hung as ear-drops; the same noun stood in the tree-list for the fruit of the tinus. e sits between the noun and its adjective in auribus e geminis, an order verse allows freely. cava tempora, “the hollow temples”, is the one detail here that belongs to the animal rather than to what has been put on him.

sentences.t:
Isque metu vacuus naturalique pavore
deposito celebrare domos mulcendaque colla
quamlibet ignotis manibus praebere solebat.
sentences.l: And he, empty of fear, his natural dread having been laid aside, was accustomed to frequent houses and to offer his neck to be stroked by hands however unknown.
sentences.i: Free of fear, his natural timidity gone, he would visit people's houses and hold out his neck to be petted by any hand at all, however strange.
sentences.n: vacuus takes the ablative metu, “empty of fear”. naturali pavore deposito is an ablative absolute, “with his natural dread laid aside”; pavor is the shying fright proper to a deer, and the phrase says the fear was not absent but put away. mulcenda colla is a gerundive with praebere: he offers his neck “to be stroked”. quamlibet ignotis is “unknown to whatever degree you please”. solebat governs both infinitives and makes the whole of it habitual.

sentences.t:
Sed tamen ante alios, Ceae pulcherrime gentis,
gratus erat, Cyparisse, tibi.
sentences.l: But still, before all others, most beautiful of the Cean race, he was dear to you, Cyparissus.
sentences.i: But more than to anyone else — loveliest of the people of Ceos — he was dear to you, Cyparissus.
sentences.n: The poet turns and speaks to the boy: pulcherrime and Cyparisse are vocatives, and the boy is named here for the first time. gratus erat ... tibi is “he was pleasing to you”, with the dative of the person pleased. Ceae ... gentis is a partitive genitive after the superlative, “most beautiful of the Cean people”; Ceae is “of Ceos”. ante alios makes the comparison with a preposition instead of a comparative.

sentences.t:
Tu pabula cervum
ad nova, tu liquidi ducebas fontis ad undam,
sentences.l: You used to lead the stag to new pasture, you to the water of a clear spring,
sentences.i: It was you who led the stag to fresh grazing, you who took him to the water of a clear spring,
sentences.n: In the first half ad follows its noun, pabula ... ad nova, the preposition tucked inside the phrase it governs. In the second it keeps its ordinary place before undam, and what is pulled apart there is the genitive, liquidi ... fontis, split around the verb. One imperfect, ducebas, serves both clauses. tu opens this clause and the two that follow, and the pronoun is doing the work: everything described from here on is the boy's doing, not the stag's.

sentences.t: tu modo nectebas varios per cornua flores,
sentences.l: at one moment you used to tie flowers of many kinds along his horns,
sentences.i: one moment you were threading all sorts of flowers through his antlers,
sentences.n: modo here is “at one moment”, and it is answered by nunc at the head of the next clause: not “now” and “now”, but “at one time” and “at another”. per cornua is “along the horns”, the flowers run through them rather than laid on top. Magnus prints nectebas, “you tied”; some editions print texebas, “you wove”, which describes the same act.

sentences.t:
nunc eques in tergo residens huc laetus et illuc
mollia purpureis frenabas ora capistris.
sentences.l: at another, seated on his back as a horseman, glad, you used to rein his soft mouth this way and that with purple halters.
sentences.i: the next, up on his back and delighted, you were reining his tender mouth first one way and then another with purple halters.
sentences.n: eques is a noun in apposition to the subject, “as a horseman”, of a boy riding a stag. residens governs in tergo, “sitting on his back”. huc ... et illuc is split around laetus, so the gladness sits inside the movement. mollia ... ora is “the soft mouth”, the plural used of a single mouth as verse often does, and purpureis ... capistris is the ablative of means. frenabas comes from frenum, the bit: the animal is being handled like a horse.

sentences.t:
Aestus erat mediusque dies, solisque vapore
concava litorei fervebant bracchia cancri:
sentences.l: There was heat and it was midday, and with the sun's vapour the hollow claws of the shore-crab were glowing:
sentences.i: It was the heat of midday, and under the sun's vapour the curved claws of the shore-crab were burning:
sentences.n: Aestus erat mediusque dies puts two nouns where English wants a clause, “there was heat, and it was the middle of the day”. The crab whose claws burn is the constellation, the sign the sun stands in at the height of summer, so the line dates the scene by the sky while keeping an animal on a beach in view; litorei, “of the shore”, holds the animal there. bracchia are properly arms, used of a crab's claws. The colon opens onto what the heat brings about.

sentences.t:
fessus in herbosa posuit sua corpora terra
cervus et arborea frigus ducebat ab umbra.
sentences.l: tired, on the grassy ground the stag laid down his body and was drawing coolness from a tree's shade.
sentences.i: worn out, the stag laid himself down on the grassy earth and drew the cool air from a tree's shade.
sentences.n: sua corpora is a plural for one body, a liberty verse takes freely. The subject cervus is held over to the following line and arrives after its own verb, so that fessus ... posuit stand before we are told who it is. frigus ducebat is “was drawing in the cool”, as one draws breath. arborea ... ab umbra brings back the noun the whole scene opened with.

sentences.t:
Hunc puer imprudens iaculo Cyparissus acuto
fixit;
sentences.l: Him the boy Cyparissus, not foreseeing it, pierced with a sharp javelin;
sentences.i: This was the stag that the boy Cyparissus, not knowing what he was aiming at, ran through with a sharp javelin;
sentences.n: Hunc, the object, stands first and keeps the stag in view from the sentence before. imprudens is “not foreseeing”, and it carries the whole accident: the boy did not know what he was throwing at. iaculo ... acuto is split around the name, the weapon closing on Cyparissus from both sides. fixit, “fixed, pierced through”, is the one verb the poem spends on the striking; the wound itself gets nothing but saevo ... vulnere in the next line, and the semicolon moves straight on.

sentences.t:
et ut saevo morientem vulnere vidit,
velle mori statuit.
sentences.l: and when he saw him dying of the savage wound, he resolved to wish to die.
sentences.i: and when he saw him dying of that cruel wound, he made up his mind that he wanted to die.
sentences.n: morientem is the object of vidit, “saw him dying”, with saevo ... vulnere, the ablative of cause, split around it. velle mori statuit is doubled on purpose: not “decided to die” but “decided to want to die”, a resolution taken about his own wishing. vidit and statuit are both perfect, and the decision comes as fast as the sight.

sentences.t:
Quae non solacia Phoebus
dixit et ut leviter pro materiaque doleret,
admonuit!
sentences.l: What consolations did Phoebus not speak, and how he urged that he should grieve lightly and in proportion to the occasion!
sentences.i: What comfort did Phoebus not offer! And how he pressed him to grieve lightly, and no more than the cause deserved!
sentences.n: Quae non solacia ... dixit is a rhetorical question that means “every consolation there was”, and the exclamation mark the edition prints stands at the end of the whole sentence, admonuit included. Phoebus is named here — the god who at line 108 was identified only by lyre and bow, and who until now has gone unnamed. ut ... doleret is the substantive clause after admonuit, “urged that he grieve”. leviter and pro materia are joined by -que: lightly, and to the measure of the thing.

sentences.t:
Gemit ille tamen munusque supremum
hoc petit a superis, ut tempore lugeat omni.
sentences.l: He groans nonetheless, and asks this from the gods above as a last gift: that he may mourn at every time.
sentences.i: Still he goes on groaning, and asks the gods above for one last gift — to be in mourning for ever.
sentences.n: Gemit and petit are presents set among the perfects around them, holding the moment open. munus supremum is “the last gift”, what is asked when nothing further will be asked. superis, “those above”, is ablative after a. ut ... lugeat is the content of the request, “that he mourn”, and tempore ... omni is pulled apart around the verb, “at all time”.

sentences.t:
Iamque per inmensos egesto sanguine fletus
in viridem verti coeperunt membra colorem,
sentences.l: And now, with his blood drained away through measureless weeping, his limbs began to be turned into a green colour,
sentences.i: And now, with his blood carried out of him by measureless weeping, his limbs began to turn green,
sentences.n: egesto sanguine is an ablative absolute, “with the blood carried out”, and per inmensos ... fletus says where it went: he weeps until there is none left. verti is the present infinitive after coeperunt. The change is put as a change of colour rather than of shape, and in viridem ... colorem is split around the verb and its subject so that “into green” and “colour” stand at the two ends of the line.

sentences.t:
et modo qui nivea pendebant fronte capilli,
horrida caesaries fieri sumptoque rigore
sidereum gracili spectare cacumine caelum.
sentences.l: and the hairs which a moment before were hanging on his snowy forehead began to become a bristling shock, and, with stiffness taken on, to look at the starry sky with a slender tip.
sentences.i: and the hair that had just been hanging over his white forehead turned into a bristling crest, and, stiffening, looked up at the starry sky in a slender point.
sentences.n: fieri and spectare still depend on the coeperunt of the line before, though their subject is capilli and not the membra of that clause. modo, “a moment ago”, sets the old state against the new. nivea ... fronte is “on the snowy forehead”, the boy's whiteness against the green just named. sumpto rigore is an ablative absolute, “with stiffness taken on”. caesaries is a head of hair and cacumen is a tree-top: the human words are kept while what they name stops being human.

sentences.t:
Ingemuit tristisque deus “lugebere nobis
lugebisque alios aderisque dolentibus” inquit.
sentences.l: The god groaned and, sorrowing, said: “You will be mourned by us, and you will mourn others, and you will be at hand for those who grieve.”
sentences.i: The god groaned, and in his grief he said: “We shall mourn you, and you shall mourn others, and you shall be at the side of those who grieve.”
sentences.n: lugebere is the second-person future ending in -re for -ris, “you will be mourned”, and nobis is the dative of the agent, “by us”, which verse allows with a plain passive. Two of the three futures are from lugeo, one passive and one active, so the boy is set first as the object of mourning and then as the one who mourns; the third, aderis, is from adsum and takes the dative dolentibus, “you will be at hand for those in grief”. The tree is being given its place at funerals, and the story ends in the god's own voice.
